title: AI, Supply Chains, and the Future of Economic Power

reader_summary.headline: Winning the AI race needs strong tech, users, and secure global supply chains.
reader_summary.overview: The episode argues that winning the AI race requires superior technology, massive user adoption, and secure supply chains. It explains how the US government uses tariffs and incentives to rebuild a hollowed-out industrial base and fix fragile global dependencies. The discussion highlights partnerships with Europe and the Middle East to build a fairer, more secure economic future.

key_points.text: The US supply chain is fragile because it relies on thousands of different vendors around the world.
key_points.evidence_quote: Our supply chains are not vertically integrated at all. They are totally geographically dispersed. Thousands of different vendors, many of them are mom-and-pop shops and different parts of the globe.

key_points.text: The US government uses tariffs to encourage companies to invest money and build technology inside the United States.
key_points.evidence_quote: Our administration has pursued an incentives-based agenda very heavily with respect to the imposition of tariffs to encourage investment in the US.

key_points.text: Tariffs corrected huge trade deficits and made it profitable again for American companies to invest in building factories and equipment.
key_points.evidence_quote: Our trade deficit was China, which has long been our largest trade deficit country has been plummeting. In a way that's really historic. Our trade deficit overall has been receding.

key_points.text: Europe struggles with high costs and bad rules, while the US offers a flexible system where companies can move to states with better conditions.
key_points.evidence_quote: And then they have the United Economics Farm where it's just really expensive to build stuff in Europe, because your energy bills are really high. You have to spend a ton of money on legal fees before you even start.

key_points.text: Middle Eastern countries have cheap energy needed for AI computing, offering a chance for American companies to collaborate and grow together.
key_points.evidence_quote: And in the Middle East, you have a lot of very cheap energy. And so that is the comparative advantage that they have identified accurately and that they want to capitalize on.

notes: Erik Torenberg sits down with Jacob Helberg to discuss AI, manufacturing, supply chains, and the new geopolitics of technology. Drawing on themes from Helberg’s book The Wires of War, they explore why hardware, industrial capacity, and secure supply chains have become central to both economic strength and national security.
